claim: The toxin of the Escherichia coli hipBA system, HipA, is a kinase that inhibits translation via phosphorylation of glutamyl-tRNA synthetase.
source: The toxin of the Escherichia coli hipBA system, HipA, is a kinase that inhibits translation via phosphorylation of glutamyl-tRNA synthetase.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Germain et al., 2013) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Enteropathogenic E. coli O127:H6 encodes the hipBA-like, tripartite TA system; hipBST, in which the HipT toxin specifically targets the tryptophanyl-tRNA synthetase, TrpS.
source: Enteropathogenic E. coli O127:H6 encodes the hipBA-like, tripartite TA system; hipBST, in which the HipT toxin specifically targets the tryptophanyl-tRNA synthetase, TrpS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Gerdes et al., 2021; Vang Nielsen et al., 2019) and represents established knowledge.

claim: In the tripartite hipBST system, the function as antitoxin has been taken over by the third protein, HipS.
source: Notably, in the tripartite system, the function as antitoxin has been taken over by the third protein, HipS, but the molecular details of how activity of HipT is inhibited remain poorly understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Vang Nielsen et al., 2019) and represents established knowledge.

claim: HipBST is structurally different from E. coli HipBA.
source: Here, we show that HipBST is structurally different from E. coli HipBA and that the unique HipS protein, which is homologous to the N-terminal subdomain of HipA, inhibits the kinase through insertion of a conserved Trp residue into the active site.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1).

claim: The unique HipS protein is homologous to the N-terminal subdomain of HipA.
source: Here, we show that HipBST is structurally different from E. coli HipBA and that the unique HipS protein, which is homologous to the N-terminal subdomain of HipA, inhibits the kinase through insertion of a conserved Trp residue into the active site.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1).

claim: HipS inhibits the HipT kinase through insertion of a conserved Trp residue into the active site.
source: Here, we show that HipBST is structurally different from E. coli HipBA and that the unique HipS protein, which is homologous to the N-terminal subdomain of HipA, inhibits the kinase through insertion of a conserved Trp residue into the active site.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data (Figure 2) and functional assays (Figure 2c).

claim: Auto-phosphorylation at two conserved sites in the kinase toxin serve different roles and affect the ability of HipS to neutralize HipT.
source: We also show how auto-phosphorylation at two conserved sites in the kinase toxin serve different roles and affect the ability of HipS to neutralize HipT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including growth assays (Figure 3a) and structural analysis (Figure 3b).

claim: Phosphorylation affects overall TA complex flexibility in solution.
source: Finally, solution structural studies show how phosphorylation affects overall TA complex flexibility.
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Canonical (type II) TA systems are small, bicistronic loci that encode a protein toxin and its cognate antidote (antitoxin) that tightly interact to form an inactive higher-order complex.
source: Canonical (type II) TA systems are small, bicistronic loci that encode a protein toxin and its cognate antidote (antitoxin) that tightly interact to form an inactive higher-order complex, usually also capable of controlling transcription via a DNA-binding domain on the antitoxin (Harms et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Harms et al., 2018) and represents established knowledge.

claim: There are examples of tricistronic TA loci, in which the third gene either encodes a chaperone required for folding of the antitoxin or an additional, transcriptional regulator.
source: However, there are also examples of tricistronic TA loci, in which the third gene either encodes a chaperone required for folding of the antitoxin and thus, toxin inhibition (Bordes et al., 2016) or an additional, transcriptional regulator (Hallez et al., 2010; Zielenkiewicz and Ceglowski, 2005; Jurėnas et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Bordes et al., 2016; Hallez et al., 2010; Zielenkiewicz and Ceglowski, 2005; Jurėnas et al., 2021).

claim: HipA is a serine–threonine kinase (STK).
source: In the widespread and diverse hipBA (high persister) system, the HipA toxin is a serine–threonine kinase (STK) (Hanks et al., 1988; Stancik et al., 2018), while the cognate antitoxin, HipB, contains a helix-turn-helix (HTH) motif (Gerdes et al., 2021; Schumacher et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hanks et al., 1988; Stancik et al., 2018).

claim: The cognate antitoxin, HipB, contains a helix-turn-helix (HTH) motif.
source: In the widespread and diverse hipBA (high persister) system, the HipA toxin is a serine–threonine kinase (STK) (Hanks et al., 1988; Stancik et al., 2018), while the cognate antitoxin, HipB, contains a helix-turn-helix (HTH) motif (Gerdes et al., 2021; Schumacher et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Gerdes et al., 2021; Schumacher et al., 2009).

claim: HipAEc specifically targets glutamyl-tRNA synthetase (GltX) by phosphorylation of an ATP-binding motif conserved in type I aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
source: For the hipBA system from Escherichia coli K-12, the toxin (HipAEc) specifically targets glutamyl-tRNA synthetase (GltX) by phosphorylation of an ATP-binding motif conserved in type I aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (Eriani et al., 1990; Sekine et al., 2003), thereby inhibiting its activity and blocking translation (Germain et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Eriani et al., 1990; Sekine et al., 2003; Germain et al., 2013).

claim: Phosphorylation of GltX by HipAEc inhibits its activity and blocks translation.
source: For the hipBA system from Escherichia coli K-12, the toxin (HipAEc) specifically targets glutamyl-tRNA synthetase (GltX) by phosphorylation of an ATP-binding motif conserved in type I aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (Eriani et al., 1990; Sekine et al., 2003), thereby inhibiting its activity and blocking translation (Germain et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Germain et al., 2013).

claim: Accumulation of uncharged tRNAGlt induces the stringent response and cellular dormancy via RelA-mediated (p)ppGpp synthesis on starved ribosomes.
source: Accumulation of uncharged tRNAGlt subsequently induces the stringent response and cellular dormancy via RelA-mediated (p)ppGpp synthesis on starved ribosomes (Haseltine and Block, 1973; Pacios et al., 2020; Winther et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Haseltine and Block, 1973; Pacios et al., 2020; Winther et al., 2018).

claim: The antitoxin, HipB, does not directly block the HipA active site.
source: In contrast to most classical type II TA systems, the antitoxin, HipB, does not directly block the HipA active site so inhibition has been proposed to occur by several alternative mechanisms, including inhibition of conformational changes in the HipA kinase required for catalysis, sequestration of HipA on DNA via the HipB DNA-binding domain (Schumacher et al., 2009), and allosterically via placement of a C-terminal Trp residue of HipB into a pocket on HipA (Evdokimov et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Schumacher et al., 2009; Evdokimov et al., 2009).

claim: HipAEc is regulated by trans auto-phosphorylation at a conserved serine (Ser150) situated in a loop near the active site termed the 'Gly-rich loop'.
source: HipAEc is also regulated by trans auto-phosphorylation at a conserved serine (Ser150) situated in a loop near the active site termed the 'Gly-rich loop' (residues 151–156), which is required for ATP binding and functionally (but not structurally) similar to the P loop of eukaryotic kinases (Huse and Kuriyan, 2002; Schumacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Huse and Kuriyan, 2002; Schumacher et al., 2012).

claim: Two discrete conformations of the Gly-rich loop are observed depending on the phosphorylation state of Ser150 and whether substrate (ATP) is bound or not.
source: Two discrete conformations of the Gly-rich loop are observed depending on the phosphorylation state of Ser150 and whether substrate (ATP) is bound or not (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2012; Schumacher et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Schumacher et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2012; Schumacher et al., 2009).

claim: In the unphosphorylated state and in the presence of ATP, the flexible Gly-rich loop is found in an inward conformation in which main chain amino groups coordinate several ATP phosphate groups and the kinase is active.
source: In the unphosphorylated state and in the presence of ATP, the flexible Gly-rich loop is found in an inward conformation in which main chain amino groups coordinate several ATP phosphate groups and the kinase is active (Schumacher et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Schumacher et al., 2009).

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser150 results in strong interactions of the phosphate group with several active sites residues, which causes ejection of the Gly-rich loop and prevents binding of ATP, thus inactivating the kinase.
source: Phosphorylation of Ser150, on the other hand, results in strong interactions of the phosphate group with several active sites residues, which causes ejection of the Gly-rich loop and prevents binding of ATP, thus inactivating the kinase (Schumacher et al., 2012; Wen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Schumacher et al., 2012; Wen et al., 2014).

claim: HipT has two phosphoserine positions, Ser57 and Ser59, in its Gly-rich loop (residues 58–63), which are both modified by trans auto-phosphorylation in vivo.
source: HipT has two phosphoserine positions, Ser57 and Ser59, in its Gly-rich loop (residues 58–63), which are both modified by trans auto-phosphorylation in vivo suggesting that they play a role in regulating the activity of HipT (Vang Nielsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Vang Nielsen et al., 2019).

claim: The crystal structure of HipBSTD233Q was determined to 2.9 Å by molecular replacement using HipAEc as search model.
source: To understand the molecular and structural basis for the functional differences between the HipBA and HipBST TA systems, we determined the crystal structure of HipBSTD233Q, containing the inactive HipT D233Q kinase variant, to 2.9 Å by molecular replacement using HipAEc as search model (Figure 1a, b, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including crystallographic methods and results.

claim: The refined structure has two copies of each of the three proteins in the asymmetric unit (ASU).
source: The refined structure (R = 19.5%, Rfree = 22.8%) has two copies of each of the three proteins in the asymmetric unit (ASU) and is generally well defined for HipB and HipT, while HipS is less well ordered.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The higher-order HipBST complex structure consists of two HipST toxin:antitoxin complexes separated by a dimer of HipB proteins.
source: The higher-order HipBST complex structure consists of two HipST toxin:antitoxin complexes separated by a dimer of HipB proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The HipBST structure differs markedly from the HipBAEc complex.
source: This differs markedly from the HipBAEc complex, in which two HipA toxins (corresponding to HipT + HipS) are closely packed head-to-tail around two HipB antitoxins (Figure 1c, top) but is reminiscent of the structure of a HipBA complex from S. oneidensis (HipBASo), which was crystallized in complex with DNA (Figure 1c, bottom) (Wen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The HipBST structure is reminiscent of the structure of a HipBA complex from S. oneidensis (HipBASo), which was crystallized in complex with DNA.
source: This differs markedly from the HipBAEc complex, in which two HipA toxins (corresponding to HipT + HipS) are closely packed head-to-tail around two HipB antitoxins (Figure 1c, top) but is reminiscent of the structure of a HipBA complex from S. oneidensis (HipBASo), which was crystallized in complex with DNA (Figure 1c, bottom) (Wen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data and citation (Wen et al., 2014).

claim: HipB consists of an α-helical bundle of four helices, including the central, DNA-binding HTH motif (residues 62–83).
source: HipB consists of an α-helical bundle of four helices, including the central, DNA-binding HTH motif (residues 62–83), which is exposed at the bridge of the hetero-hexamer (Figure 1b, green).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The helical bundle of HipB is followed by a small β strand that forms an antiparallel sheet by pairing with the corresponding stretch in the neighbouring HipB protein, thus forming a homodimer.
source: The helical bundle is followed by a small β strand that forms an antiparallel sheet by pairing with the corresponding stretch in the neighbouring HipB protein, thus forming a homodimer.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The N-terminus of HipB (residues 1–35) is not visible in the electron density.
source: The N-terminus of HipB (residues 1–35) is not visible in the electron density, but AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021) prediction indicates that it forms a single α-helix (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and computational prediction.

claim: AlphaFold2 prediction indicates that the N-terminus of HipB forms a single α-helix.
source: The N-terminus of HipB (residues 1–35) is not visible in the electron density, but AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021) prediction indicates that it forms a single α-helix (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational prediction using AlphaFold2.

claim: HipB from HipBST does not have a C-terminal hydrophobic residue that reaches a cleft between the N-subdomain 1 and the core kinase domain.
source: For HipBAEc, a hydrophobic residue at the C-terminus of HipB was proposed to reach a cleft between the N-subdomain 1 and the core kinase domain of HipA and inhibit activity by restricting domain movements required for catalysis (Figure 1c; Schumacher et al., 2009). HipB from HipBST does not have such a C-terminal residue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), supporting that HipB functions as a transcriptional regulator rather than the antitoxin.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and structural comparison.

claim: Expression of HipBSTD233Q or HipB alone efficiently repressed transcription from the hipBST promoter.
source: Expression of HipBSTD233Q or HipB alone efficiently repressed transcription, while expression of either HipS or HipTD233Q alone did not affect transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of either HipS or HipTD233Q alone did not affect transcription from the hipBST promoter.
source: Expression of HipBSTD233Q or HipB alone efficiently repressed transcription, while expression of either HipS or HipTD233Q alone did not affect transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: hipB is required, and sufficient, for transcriptional repression of the hipBST promoter.
source: Thus, hipB is required, and sufficient, for transcriptional repression of the hipBST promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: HipT has several conserved, positively charged residues near the expected location of the DNA phosphodiester backbone.
source: With respect to DNA binding, superposition of HipBST with HipBASo in complex with DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a) shows that HipT has several conserved, positively charged residues near the expected location of the DNA phosphodiester backbone, supporting that HipBST binds DNA in a similar way to HipBASo.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: HipBST binds DNA in a similar way to HipBASo.
source: With respect to DNA binding, superposition of HipBST with HipBASo in complex with DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a) shows that HipT has several conserved, positively charged residues near the expected location of the DNA phosphodiester backbone, supporting that HipBST binds DNA in a similar way to HipBASo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural comparison and the presence of conserved residues.

claim: HipS interacts tightly with HipT in the HipBST complex.
source: HipS interacts tightly with HipT in the HipBST complex and consists of a solvent-facing, five-stranded anti-parallel β sheet of which four strands are located in the N terminus (residues 1–52).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: HipS consists of a solvent-facing, five-stranded anti-parallel β sheet of which four strands are located in the N terminus (residues 1–52).
source: HipS interacts tightly with HipT in the HipBST complex and consists of a solvent-facing, five-stranded anti-parallel β sheet of which four strands are located in the N terminus (residues 1–52).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: A small domain of three helices (residues 53–94) in HipS forms the interface to HipT.
source: A small domain of three helices (residues 53–94) forms the interface to HipT and is followed by the fifth β strand (residues 95–102, Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The fold of the HipST heterodimer is structurally very similar to the longer HipA kinase, such as HipAEc.
source: As expected from sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), the fold of the HipST heterodimer is structurally very similar to the longer HipA kinase, such as HipAEc (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: HipS is structurally homologous to the N-subdomain 1 of HipA.
source: In other words, HipS is structurally homologous to the N-subdomain 1 of HipA (Schumacher et al., 2012), both with respect to its overall fold and to its orientation with respect to the core kinase domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data and citation (Schumacher et al., 2012).

claim: The HipS C-terminus overlaps with an extended linker that bridges N-subdomains 1 and 2 in HipA.
source: However, the HipS C-terminus overlaps with an extended linker that bridges N-subdomains 1 and 2 in HipA (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: HipT corresponds structurally to the core kinase domain of HipA, except for an additional N-terminal mini-domain (residues 1–41).
source: HipT, on its part, corresponds structurally to the core kinase domain of HipA, except for an additional N-terminal mini-domain of unknown significance (residues 1–41, Figure 1a, e).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 1a, e.

claim: In the HipBSTD233Q structure, the Gly-rich loop of HipT is found in an outward-facing conformation despite the absence of Gly-rich loop phosphorylation.
source: Finally, in this structure, the Gly-rich loop of HipT is found in an outward-facing conformation despite the absence of Gly-rich loop phosphorylation, suggesting that HipT is inactive (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d.

claim: The outward-facing conformation of the Gly-rich loop in HipT suggests that HipT is inactive.
source: Finally, in this structure, the Gly-rich loop of HipT is found in an outward-facing conformation despite the absence of Gly-rich loop phosphorylation, suggesting that HipT is inactive (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural data and comparison with known inactive conformations.

claim: There are three major areas of contact between HipT and HipS in the HipBST complex, involving both hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic and charged interactions.
source: There are three major areas of contact between the two proteins in the HipBST complex, involving both hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic and charged interactions (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: HipT and HipS interact directly very close to the Gly-rich loop, where Glu63 from HipS points directly into the HipT active site.
source: Importantly, HipT and HipS were found to interact directly very close to the Gly-rich loop, where Glu63 from HipS points directly into the HipT active site while HipS Trp65 is wedged into a deep cavity formed by the Gly-rich loop in its outward conformation (Figure 2a, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: HipS Trp65 is wedged into a deep cavity formed by the Gly-rich loop in its outward conformation.
source: Importantly, HipT and HipS were found to interact directly very close to the Gly-rich loop, where Glu63 from HipS points directly into the HipT active site while HipS Trp65 is wedged into a deep cavity formed by the Gly-rich loop in its outward conformation (Figure 2a, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Glu63 is conserved in the N-subdomain 1 of the longer HipA toxins.
source: Of these, Glu63 is conserved in the N-subdomain 1 of the longer HipA toxins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), and therefore less likely contribute to functional differences between the two systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Trp65 is found in many HipS orthologues.
source: Trp65, on the other hand, is found in many HipS orthologues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and moreover, the region surrounding it is both structurally and electrostatically different from the corresponding region in HipAEc (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The region surrounding Trp65 is both structurally and electrostatically different from the corresponding region in HipAEc.
source: Trp65, on the other hand, is found in many HipS orthologues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and moreover, the region surrounding it is both structurally and electrostatically different from the corresponding region in HipAEc (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Insertion of the bulky Trp residue near the HipT active site might sterically block transition of the Gly-rich loop from its outward to the inward conformation.
source: Based on this, we hypothesized that insertion of the bulky Trp residue near the HipT active site might sterically block transition of the Gly-rich loop from its outward to the inward conformation, likely required for ATP binding and kinase activity.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: Wild-type HipS, but not HipSW65A, can neutralize toxicity of HipT in vivo.
source: Dilution spot assays confirmed that wt HipS, but not HipSW65A, can neutralize toxicity of HipT in vivo (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: HipS neutralizes the kinase by insertion of a conserved tryptophan residue, likely preventing structural transition from the inactive to the active conformation.
source: In conclusion, we show that HipS interacts directly with the HipT active site and neutralizes the kinase by insertion of a conserved tryptophan residue, likely preventing structural transition from the inactive to the active conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data (Figure 2a, b) and functional assays (Figure 2c).

claim: Both wild-type HipT (S57IS59; SIS), as well as HipT D57IS59 (DIS) and S57ID59 (SID), caused growth inhibition upon overexpression in E. coli MG1655.
source: Growth assays in liquid culture showed that both wild-type HipT (S57IS59; SIS), as well as HipT D57IS59 (DIS) and S57ID59 (SID), caused growth inhibition upon overexpression in E. coli MG1655 (Figure 3a), demonstrating that the phosphomimetic mutations do not prevent toxicity, and consequently, kinase activity of HipT towards its target.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The phosphomimetic mutations do not prevent toxicity, and consequently, kinase activity of HipT towards its target.
source: Growth assays in liquid culture showed that both wild-type HipT (S57IS59; SIS), as well as HipT D57IS59 (DIS) and S57ID59 (SID), caused growth inhibition upon overexpression in E. coli MG1655 (Figure 3a), demonstrating that the phosphomimetic mutations do not prevent toxicity, and consequently, kinase activity of HipT towards its target.
evidence: This claim is inferred from growth assay data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Co-expression of HipS neutralized the toxicity of HipT SIS and SID variants.
source: In addition, while co-expression of HipS neutralized the toxicity of HipT SIS and SID variants, the antitoxin was unable to neutralize the toxicity of the HipT DIS variant, suggesting that Ser57, but not Ser59, negatively impacts the function of HipS as antitoxin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: HipS was unable to neutralize the toxicity of the HipT DIS variant.
source: In addition, while co-expression of HipS neutralized the toxicity of HipT SIS and SID variants, the antitoxin was unable to neutralize the toxicity of the HipT DIS variant, suggesting that Ser57, but not Ser59, negatively impacts the function of HipS as antitoxin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Ser57, but not Ser59, negatively impacts the function of HipS as antitoxin.

evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Alanine substitutions at either Ser position almost (S57IA59; SIA) or completely (A57IS59; AIS) abolished HipT toxicity.
source: Finally, alanine substitutions at either Ser position almost (S57IA59; SIA) or completely (A57IS59; AIS) abolished HipT toxicity (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Both serine residues (in either phosphorylation state) are important for HipT toxicity.
source: Thus, both serine residues (in either phosphorylation state) are important for HipT toxicity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser57 negatively affects the function of HipS as antitoxin under conditions where the HipT kinase is toxic.
source: In summary, we find that phosphorylation of Ser57 negatively affects the function of HipS as antitoxin under conditions where the HipT kinase is toxic.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser57 in HipT represents a clear functional departure from HipA, where phosphorylation of Ser150 inactivates the toxin.
source: This represents a clear functional departure from HipA, where phosphorylation of Ser150 inactivates the toxin (Schumacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior work (Schumacher et al., 2012).

claim: Two additional crystal structures of the HipBST complex were determined in context of the HipT AIS (2.4 Å) and SIA (3.4 Å) variants.
source: To understand how phosphorylation of the two serine residues affects the structure of the HipBST complex, we determined two additional crystal structures of the HipBST complex in context of the HipT AIS (2.4 Å) and SIA (3.4 Å) variants (Supplementary file 1a), which are non-toxic in vivo, but in principle maintain an intact kinase active site.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: For the HipBST AIS variant, phosphorylation of Ser59 was found in both copies of HipT in the crystallographic ASU.
source: For the HipBST AIS variant, we found a strong peak corresponding to phosphorylation of Ser59 in both copies of HipT in the crystallographic ASU (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), while for the HipBST SIA variant, phosphorylation of Ser57 was present but incomplete and could only be confidently modelled in one of the two HipT molecules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: For the HipBST SIA variant, phosphorylation of Ser57 was present but incomplete and could only be confidently modelled in one of the two HipT molecules.
source: For the HipBST AIS variant, we found a strong peak corresponding to phosphorylation of Ser59 in both copies of HipT in the crystallographic ASU (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), while for the HipBST SIA variant, phosphorylation of Ser57 was present but incomplete and could only be confidently modelled in one of the two HipT molecules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: In its phosphorylated state, Ser59 (P-Ser59) forms strong interactions to Lys161, His212, as well as to the catalytic Asp210 inside the active site.
source: In its phosphorylated state, Ser59 (P-Ser59) forms strong interactions to Lys161, His212, as well as to the catalytic Asp210 inside the active site (Figure 3b, top), while P-Ser57 is located further away and forms hydrogen bonds to Tyr162 and Asp210 (Figure 3b, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: P-Ser57 is located further away and forms hydrogen bonds to Tyr162 and Asp210.
source: In its phosphorylated state, Ser59 (P-Ser59) forms strong interactions to Lys161, His212, as well as to the catalytic Asp210 inside the active site (Figure 3b, top), while P-Ser57 is located further away and forms hydrogen bonds to Tyr162 and Asp210 (Figure 3b, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The Gly-rich loop maintains an outward conformation in both HipBST AIS and SIA structures similar to the one observed before, likely incompatible with ATP binding.
source: Nevertheless, the Gly-rich loop maintains an outward conformation in both structures similar to the one observed before, likely incompatible with ATP binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: HipT is inactive in the context of the HipBST complex regardless of the phosphorylation state of the serine residues in the Gly-rich loop.
source: Taken together, the structures suggest that HipT is inactive in the context of the HipBST complex regardless of the phosphorylation state of the serine residues in the Gly-rich loop.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural data.

claim: This is distinctly different from HipA, where phosphorylation of Ser150 was found to convert the kinase from an active to an inactive form by causing ejection of the Gly-rich loop.
source: This is distinctly different from HipA, where phosphorylation of Ser150 was found to convert the kinase from an active to an inactive form by causing ejection of the Gly-rich loop (Schumacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior work (Schumacher et al., 2012).

claim: Analysis on Phos-tag gels confirmed that HipT AIS primarily is found on the phosphorylated form.
source: This experiment confirmed that HipT AIS primarily is found on the phosphorylated form (Figure 3c, upper band), while HipT SIA is mostly on the unphosphorylated form (Figure 3c, lower band), thus in both cases consistent with the structural analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: HipT SIA is mostly on the unphosphorylated form.
source: This experiment confirmed that HipT AIS primarily is found on the phosphorylated form (Figure 3c, upper band), while HipT SIA is mostly on the unphosphorylated form (Figure 3c, lower band), thus in both cases consistent with the structural analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Phosphorylation of neither of the two phosphoserine positions in HipT affects the conformation of the Gly-rich loop in the context of the HipBST complex.
source: In summary, we conclude that phosphorylation of neither of the two phosphoserine positions in HipT affects the conformation of the Gly-rich loop in the context of the HipBST complex, where the loop remains in an outward conformation in all cases suggesting the kinase is not in its canonical, activated state.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural data.

claim: Auto-phosphorylation still takes place in both the SIA and AIS variants demonstrating that the kinase is still active.
source: Surprisingly, auto-phosphorylation still takes place in both the SIA and AIS variants demonstrating that the kinase is still active and consequently, that the lack of toxicity observed for these variants likely relates to target binding rather than kinase inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data (Figure 3b) and Phos-tag gel data (Figure 3c).

claim: The lack of toxicity observed for the SIA and AIS variants likely relates to target binding rather than kinase inactivation.
source: Surprisingly, auto-phosphorylation still takes place in both the SIA and AIS variants demonstrating that the kinase is still active and consequently, that the lack of toxicity observed for these variants likely relates to target binding rather than kinase inactivation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the kinase is still active but not toxic.

claim: The position of the Ser59 phosphate group in the AIS variant (HipTS57A) corresponds closely to that of the gamma-phosphate of ATP inside the active site of HipA.
source: Finally, we note that the position of the Ser59 phosphate group in the AIS variant (HipTS57A) corresponds closely to that of the gamma-phosphate of ATP inside the active site of HipA, suggesting that phosphorylation in fact may stabilize the active site in a similar way to ATP (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser59 may stabilize the active site in a similar way to ATP.
source: Finally, we note that the position of the Ser59 phosphate group in the AIS variant (HipTS57A) corresponds closely to that of the gamma-phosphate of ATP inside the active site of HipA, suggesting that phosphorylation in fact may stabilize the active site in a similar way to ATP (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural comparison.

claim: For the protein purified with the wild-type SIS Gly-rich loop, the band corresponding to HipS was missing.
source: Intriguingly, for the protein purified with the wild-type SIS Gly-rich loop, the band corresponding to HipS was missing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Analysis of the purified samples of the three variants by SAXS gave very similar intensity curves suggesting that the complexes have similar sizes and shapes in solution.
source: Analysis of the purified samples of the three variants by small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) gave very similar intensity curves suggesting that the complexes have similar sizes and shapes in solution, despite the missing HipS protein in the SIS variant (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: All Guinier plots show a linear behaviour at low angles demonstrating the absence of large aggregates.
source: Moreover, all Guinier plots show a linear behaviour at low angles demonstrating the absence of large aggregates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b) while the indirect Fourier transformation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c) and pair distance distribution functions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d) support similar, overall structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The maximum diameter of 200 Å is significantly larger than the crystal structure (max. diameter 135 Å).
source: Interestingly, the maximum diameter of 200 Å is significantly larger than the crystal structure (max. diameter 135 Å), consistent with analysis of the forward scattering that revealed partial oligomerization of the samples with an average mass corresponding to roughly a dimer of the HipBST heterohexamer.
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data analysis.

claim: Analysis of the forward scattering revealed partial oligomerization of the samples with an average mass corresponding to roughly a dimer of the HipBST heterohexamer.
source: Interestingly, the maximum diameter of 200 Å is significantly larger than the crystal structure (max. diameter 135 Å), consistent with analysis of the forward scattering that revealed partial oligomerization of the samples with an average mass corresponding to roughly a dimer of the HipBST heterohexamer.
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data analysis.

claim: The normalized Kratky plot agrees with a relatively compact structure without significant random coil content.
source: Finally, the normalized Kratky plot agrees with a relatively compact structure without significant random coil content (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: SAXS data from the HipT SIS variant were matched very well by a model in which HipS was omitted and the disordered N-terminus of HipB was included as a helical element.
source: Consistent with the biochemical data, the SAXS data from the HipT SIS variant were matched very well by a model in which HipS was omitted and the disordered N-terminus of HipB was included as a helical element (Figure 4, blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS modeling data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the SIS structure model, the two HipT modules have rotated slightly to open up the cleft between them as compared to the crystal structure.
source: In this structure, the two HipT modules have rotated slightly to open up the cleft between them as compared to the crystal structure (Figure 4b, blue, arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS modeling data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Data measured for both the SID and DIS variants both matched the complete HipBST crystal structure (with the N-terminal HipB extension) with only minor adjustments of the domains.
source: On the contrary, data measured for both the SID (Figure 4a, b, red) and DIS (Figure 4a, b, orange) variants both matched the complete HipBST crystal structure (with the N-terminal HipB extension) with only minor adjustments of the domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS modeling data shown in Figure 4a, b.

claim: SAXS analysis suggests that the HipBST complex is dynamic in solution in a phosphoserine-dependent way.
source: Taken together, SAXS analysis suggests that the HipBST complex is dynamic in solution in a phosphoserine-dependent way and that the phosphorylation state of HipT influences the inhibitory function of HipS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from SAXS data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The phosphorylation state of HipT influences the inhibitory function of HipS.
source: Taken together, SAXS analysis suggests that the HipBST complex is dynamic in solution in a phosphoserine-dependent way and that the phosphorylation state of HipT influences the inhibitory function of HipS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from SAXS data and functional assays.

claim: This dynamic behaviour likely explains how it is possible for the inactivated HipBST TA complex to undergo auto-phosphorylation in vivo.
source: This dynamic behaviour likely explains how it is possible for the inactivated HipBST TA complex to undergo auto-phosphorylation in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from SAXS data and functional observations.

claim: A phylogenetic tree of the 48 known HipT orthologues in bacterial genomes largely separates the kinases by the configuration of the Gly-rich loop.
source: Finally, we wanted to understand if Gly-rich loops with two phosphoserine positions are common among HipT-like kinases. For this, we generated a phylogenetic tree of the 48 known HipT orthologues in bacterial genomes (Gerdes et al., 2021; Figure 5a). Interestingly, investigation of this tree revealed that it largely separates the kinases by the configuration of the Gly-rich loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The largest branch, the SΨS group, contains HipT kinases with two serine residues separated by a small aliphatic amino acid.
source: The largest branch, which we named the SΨS group, contains HipT kinases with two serine residues separated by a small aliphatic amino acid, corresponding to the known auto-phosphorylation sites in HipT of E. coli O127:H6, Ser57 and Ser59 (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The second Ser/Thr position appears less conserved than the first.
source: Overall, the second Ser/Thr position appears less conserved than the first, and some kinases even contain a proline (P) or glutamine (Q) here, suggesting different regulation patterns for different HipT kinases with Ser57 playing a more important role.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5a, b.

claim: Ser57 plays a more important role than Ser59 in HipT regulation.
source: Overall, the second Ser/Thr position appears less conserved than the first, and some kinases even contain a proline (P) or glutamine (Q) here, suggesting different regulation patterns for different HipT kinases with Ser57 playing a more important role.
evidence: This claim is inferred from phylogenetic analysis and functional data.

claim: A large fraction of HipT kinases contain a conserved SΨS motif with two potential phosphorylation positions in their Gly-rich loops.
source: In summary, phylogenetic analysis reveals that a large fraction of HipT kinases contain a conserved SΨS motif with two potential phosphorylation positions in their Gly-rich loops, supporting that both Ser59, and in particular Ser57, play an important role in the regulation of the HipBST TA system.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both Ser59, and in particular Ser57, play an important role in the regulation of the HipBST TA system.
source: In summary, phylogenetic analysis reveals that a large fraction of HipT kinases contain a conserved SΨS motif with two potential phosphorylation positions in their Gly-rich loops, supporting that both Ser59, and in particular Ser57, play an important role in the regulation of the HipBST TA system.
evidence: This claim is inferred from phylogenetic analysis and functional data.

claim: The crystal structure of the kinase-inactive HipBSTD233Q complex shows that HipS interacts in a similar way to the corresponding N-subdomain 1 in HipA.
source: In this study, we present a detailed structural and functional analysis of the tripartite HipBST TA system from enteropathogenic E. coli O127:H6, which elucidates the neutralizing mechanism of the unusual HipS antitoxin and dissects the functional roles of the two phosphoserine residues in HipT, Ser57 and Ser59. The crystal structure of the kinase-inactive HipBSTD233Q complex shows that HipS interacts in a similar way to the corresponding N-subdomain 1 in HipA but neutralizes HipT by direction interaction involving insertion a large, bulky residue, Trp65, into the kinase active site.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: HipS neutralizes HipT by direction interaction involving insertion a large, bulky residue, Trp65, into the kinase active site.
source: In this study, we present a detailed structural and functional analysis of the tripartite HipBST TA system from enteropathogenic E. coli O127:H6, which elucidates the neutralizing mechanism of the unusual HipS antitoxin and dissects the functional roles of the two phosphoserine residues in HipT, Ser57 and Ser59. The crystal structure of the kinase-inactive HipBSTD233Q complex shows that HipS interacts in a similar way to the corresponding N-subdomain 1 in HipA but neutralizes HipT by direction interaction involving insertion a large, bulky residue, Trp65, into the kinase active site.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data (Figure 2) and functional assays (Figure 2c).

claim: Trp65 is conserved in some, but not all HipS proteins.
source: Trp65 is conserved in some, but not all HipS proteins, and is located in a motif that differs both structurally and at the sequence level from the corresponding region in HipA, which is otherwise very similar to HipS (Gerdes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and citation (Gerdes et al., 2021).

claim: The structural basis for the role of HipS as antitoxin in the HipBST system involves preventing the Gly-rich loop from transitioning from the outward, inactive state, to a conformation compatible with ATP binding.
source: Together, this suggests that the structural basis for the role of HipS as antitoxin in the HipBST system involves preventing the Gly-rich loop from transitioning from the outward, inactive state, to a conformation compatible with ATP binding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural and functional data.

claim: In some organisms, the residue corresponding to Trp65 is a proline, which may point to yet another way of preventing activation.
source: In some organisms, the residue corresponding to Trp65 is a proline, which may point to yet another way of preventing activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is inferred from sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Structures of a HipT orthologue from Legionella pneumophila (HipTLp) in complex with either the non-hydrolyzable ATP analogue (AMPPNP) or the equivalent of E. coli HipS, HipSLp as well as the isolated structure of a HipS from Haemophilus influenzae have been determined.
source: Recently, structures of a HipT orthologue from Legionella pneumophila (HipTLp) in complex with either the non-hydrolyzable ATP analogue (AMPPNP) or the equivalent of E. coli HipS, HipSLp as well as the isolated structure of a HipS from Haemophilus influenzae have been determined (Lin et al., 2023; Zhen et al., 2022; Koo et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Lin et al., 2023; Zhen et al., 2022; Koo et al., 2022).

claim: HipTEc and HipTLp differ significantly in the structure and size of the loops that were proposed to engage in target binding.
source: HipTEc and HipTLp differ significantly in the structure and size of the loops that were proposed to engage in target binding (Gerdes et al., 2021) suggesting that the two Hip kinases might have different targets (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation (Gerdes et al., 2021).

claim: The two Hip kinases (HipTEc and HipTLp) might have different targets.
source: HipTEc and HipTLp differ significantly in the structure and size of the loops that were proposed to engage in target binding (Gerdes et al., 2021) suggesting that the two Hip kinases might have different targets (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural differences.

claim: The N-terminal minidomain that stretches from the N-terminus to the start of the Gly-rich loop is unresolved in the HipSTLp structure whilst being visible in the isolated structure of the HipTLp toxin.
source: Moreover, the N-terminal minidomain that stretches from the N-terminus to the start of the Gly-rich loop is unresolved in the HipSTLp structure whilst being visible in the isolated structure of the HipTLp toxin.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The N-terminal minidomain region is ordered in the structure of E. coli HipBST, which also suggests that the two kinases differ.
source: This region is ordered in the structure of E. coli HipBST, which also suggests that the two kinases differ.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: HipTLp belongs to the SΨQ group, and phosphorylation of the Gly-rich loop can thus take place only at the position corresponding to Ser57 in HipTEc.
source: HipTLp belongs to the SΨQ group, and phosphorylation of the Gly-rich loop can thus take place only at the position corresponding to Ser57 in HipTEc.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and structural data.

claim: HipTLp is found with its active site loop in an inward and active conformation with nucleotide bound, despite being phosphorylated.
source: Interestingly, and despite being phosphorylated, HipTLp is found with its active site loop in an inward and active conformation with nucleotide bound.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from prior work.

claim: In HipTLp, the phosphoserine moiety is stabilized by two conserved arginine residues in a RxDR motif, which is found both in HipTEc and HipAEc.
source: In this conformation, the phosphoserine moiety is stabilized by two conserved arginine residues in a RxDR motif, which is found both in HipTEc and HipAEc (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and sequence analysis.

claim: In HipA, the Gly-rich loop does not contact the RxDR motif in either phosphorylation state, suggesting that this interaction is a unique feature of HipT kinases.
source: In HipA, however, the Gly-rich loop does not contact the RxDR motif in either phosphorylation state, suggesting that this interaction is a unique feature of HipT kinases (Schumacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison and citation (Schumacher et al., 2012).

claim: Gln56 in HipTLp, which corresponds to Ser59 in HipTEc, interacts with two residues, Asp145 and Lys201.
source: Gln56 (SΨQ), which corresponds to Ser59 in HipTEc and arguably in some respects mimics a phosphorylated serine, interacts with two residues, Asp145 and Lys201.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from prior work.

claim: Asp145 and Lys201 in HipTLp have chemically similar counterparts in HipTEc (Gln151 and Arg214).
source: These have chemically similar counterparts in HipTEc (Gln151 and Arg214) and thus might interact with the phosphorylated Ser59 when the Gly-rich loop is in its inward state, that is, in the absence of HipS.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: Interactions at both sites (Ser57 to the RxDR motif, Ser59 to Gln151/Arg214) would stabilize the loop in its inward state and possibly affect the function of HipS as antitoxin.
source: Interactions at both sites (Ser57 to the RxDR motif, Ser59 to Gln151/Arg214) would stabilize the loop in its inward state and possibly affect the function of HipS as antitoxin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: The serine residues in the HipT Gly-rich loop (Ser57 and Ser59) are important for toxicity but apparently not for auto-phosphorylation.
source: Finally, we show that the serine residues in the HipT Gly-rich loop (Ser57 and Ser59) are important for toxicity but apparently not for auto-phosphorylation as we observe auto-phosphorylation in both the AIS and SIA variants of HipT.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays (Figure 3a) and structural data (Figure 3b, c).

claim: Auto-phosphorylation serves to both control target (TrpS) phosphorylation and HipS binding.
source: This is compatible with a model in which auto-phosphorylation serves to both control target (TrpS) phosphorylation and HipS binding, which could explain the need for two sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from functional and structural data.

claim: The molecular mechanism controlling at which site auto-phosphorylation takes places is still not known.
source: The molecular mechanism controlling at which site auto-phosphorylation takes places is still not known, but the structures of HipBST AIS and HipBST SIA suggest that subtle changes in the loop can affect this (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Residues involved in both ATP binding and catalysis, the phosphoserine residues in the Gly-rich loop, and parts of HipS form a tightly interconnected network of interactions.
source: Together, our data support a complex network model for the interplay between the active site and the Gly-rich loop depicted in Figure 6. In this model, residues involved in both ATP binding and catalysis, the phosphoserine residues in the Gly-rich loop, and parts of HipS form a tightly interconnected network of interactions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural and functional data.

claim: Posttranslational modification and/or mutation of any single residue can have multiple downstream effects.
source: The result of this complexity is that posttranslational modification and/or mutation of any single residue can have multiple downstream effects.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the complex network model.

claim: Inactivation of the HipT active site through the D210A mutation appears to also affects the position of the Gly-rich loop as well as HipS binding, via direct interactions to the serine residues.
source: For example, inactivation of the HipT active site through the D210A mutation appears to also affects the position of the Gly-rich loop as well as HipS binding, via direct interactions to the serine residues.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural and biochemical data.

claim: The position of the Gly-rich loop and binding of HipS are mutually interconnected so that HipS controls whether the loop can transition from an outward to an inward state.
source: Likewise, the position of the Gly-rich loop and binding of HipS are mutually interconnected so that HipS controls whether the loop can transition from an outward to an inward state and conversely, the serine residues and their phosphorylation state likely also control with what affinity HipS binds.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural and functional data.

claim: The serine residues and their phosphorylation state likely also control with what affinity HipS binds.
source: Likewise, the position of the Gly-rich loop and binding of HipS are mutually interconnected so that HipS controls whether the loop can transition from an outward to an inward state and conversely, the serine residues and their phosphorylation state likely also control with what affinity HipS binds.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural and functional data.

claim: The role of HipS shifts from that of a classical antitoxin that simply blocks and inhibits the toxin active site to that of an allosteric enzymatic modulator.
source: This shifts the role of HipS from that of a classical antitoxin that simply blocks and inhibits the toxin active site to that of an allosteric enzymatic modulator.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural and functional data.
